decisions.note: Role resolved: both anchors are include/crypto/ed25519_algebra/ed25519_algebra.h:71 and src/common/crypto/ed25519_algebra/ed25519_algebra.c — the Ed25519 group and field arithmetic layer that the EdDSA and FROST cosigners are built on, not an independent key use. It belongs in the inventory because a post-quantum scheme replaces this layer wholesale, but it is the same exposure as the threshold EdDSA rows reached one level lower, so it must not be counted as additional surface.

The largest row in this repository by reference count — 911 references across 30 files — and the one a post-quantum signature standard does not address. The anchors run through the BAM ECDSA cosigner surface (include/cosigner/bam_ecdsa_cosigner{,_client,_server}.h) and, importantly, through the key persistency structures (bam_key_persistency_structures{,_client,_server}.h): Paillier material is not only used in the protocol, it is *stored*. That matters for sequencing, because stored ciphertext is a harvest-now-decrypt-later item while a protocol is only a future-signing item. Replacing Paillier means redesigning the threshold protocol, not swapping a primitive: NIST's 2024 standards are single-signer, its multi-party threshold call is still open, and the literature notes PQC-round schemes do not convert directly to threshold form through MPC.

Correct, anchored on a real implementation (include/crypto/commitments/pedersen.h) plus the cosigner clients and servers that use it and the key persistency structures that store it. Stated precisely: breaking the discrete log costs a Pedersen commitment its binding property, not its hiding — it is perfectly hiding, so committed values are not recoverable even with a CRQC. The exposure is forgeability within the proofs, which is future soundness rather than retroactive disclosure. Do not describe this row as "amounts become readable".

Correct and well anchored, unlike the equivalent row in cb-mpc: the files are the CMP signing services themselves (include/cosigner/cmp_ecdsa_{offline,online,}_signing_service.h and src/common/cosigner/cmp_ecdsa_offline_signing_service.cpp), i.e. an implementation of the CMP/CGGMP threshold ECDSA protocol. This is the core custody operation: every transaction the cosigner authorises goes through it.

Correct: include/cosigner/frost_cosigner{,_client,_server}.h and platform_service.h, 70 references. FROST is a Schnorr-based threshold signature over a prime-order group, so Shor breaks it by the same discrete-log attack as the ECDSA protocols — worth a separate row because FROST is often presented as the modern, safer choice, and its quantum exposure is identical. There is no post-quantum FROST analogue in production.

Threshold EdDSA signing: src/common/cosigner/asymmetric_eddsa_cosigner_server.cpp:401, eddsa_online_signing_service.cpp and frost_cosigner_server.cpp. Same migration class as the FROST and threshold-ECDSA rows.

include/cosigner/sign_algorithm.h:10 — the enumeration of supported signing algorithms. A small row, and the right one to look at first in a migration: the place where a new scheme has to be admitted into the protocol's type system, and therefore a version-compatibility problem across every deployed cosigner.

findings.title: Quantum-vulnerable Paillier: threshold signing and MPC protocols (30 file(s))
findings.description: 911 reference(s) to Paillier across 30 file(s), e.g. include/cosigner/bam_ecdsa_cosigner.h:59. Role, judged from paths, function names and nearby code: threshold signing and MPC protocols. Paillier, Pedersen commitments and the discrete-logarithm proofs inside threshold ECDSA and EdDSA protocols all fall to Shor's algorithm; a post-quantum threshold scheme is a protocol change, not a parameter change.
findings.impact: Long-term risk depends on what the algorithm protects: signatures (authenticity until migration) or key exchange/encryption (retroactive decryption of recorded data).
findings.recommendation: Track post-quantum threshold signatures (NIST IR 8214C) and keep the protocol layer ready to swap the signature scheme; record which keys and shares must stay valid for how long.
findings.limitations: This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Heuristic pattern match on source text without data-flow analysis. The usage context (security-relevant or not) must be confirmed manually; treat as preliminary.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — factoring
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Breaks RSA at every key length: a longer modulus only raises the cost polynomially. Plan migration to ML-KEM (or a hybrid) for key establishment and ML-DSA / SLH-DSA for signatures; start with keys protecting data that must stay confidential for years (harvest now, decrypt later) and with long-lived signatures.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Needs a fault-tolerant quantum computer. Published estimates for RSA-2048 fell from 20 million noisy qubits and 8 hours (Gidney–Ekerå 2021) to under a million noisy qubits and under a week (Gidney 2025); a 2026 neutral-atom design puts RSA-2048 one to two orders of magnitude slower than P-256 on 26,000 qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions; no such machine is publicly known.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — discrete logarithms in finite fields
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Breaks finite-field Diffie–Hellman and DSA at every size. Move key establishment to ML-KEM (hybrid with X25519 or ECDH during the transition) and signatures to ML-DSA or SLH-DSA.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Gidney–Ekerå (2021) estimate RSA and finite-field discrete logarithms together; the resources are of the same order. Ekerå–Gärtner (2024) compare the current algorithm variants for safe-prime and Schnorr groups.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: 2026 estimates for a 256-bit curve: under 1,200 logical qubits and 90 million Toffoli gates, under half a million physical superconducting qubits running for minutes (Babbush et al.); 1,193 logical qubits with more gates (Chevignard–Fouque–Schrottenloher); P-256 in a few days on 26,000 neutral-atom qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions, not forecasts.

quantum_algorithms.name: Grover's algorithm — key search and preimages
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Not a break. 256-bit keys (AES-256, ChaCha20) keep a comfortable margin; AES-128 meets NIST category 1, while some authorities ask for 256-bit keys in quantum-resistant contexts (see the AES-128 entry). Prefer 256-bit keys for long-lived data; 256-bit hashes need no change for preimage resistance.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: The search is long and serial: NIST counts AES-128 key search as 2^170/MAXDEPTH quantum gates with MAXDEPTH between 2^40 and 2^96 and uses it as the yardstick of security category 1; a SHA-256 preimage was estimated at about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles on 2^12.6 logical qubits (Amy et al. 2016).

quantum_algorithms.name: Brassard–Høyer–Tapp — collision search
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: 256-bit hashes (SHA-256, SHA3-256) remain adequate for collision resistance; 160-bit hashes are already weak classically (SHA-1 collisions are practical). Use 384/512-bit hashes where NIST categories 4–5 are required.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Bernstein (2009) argued that, once hardware cost is counted, it is not cheaper than classical parallel collision search; NIST defines security category 2 by SHA3-256 collision search counted in classical gates (2^146).

scenario.rationale: Inside the 10-year horizon the survey puts at 28-49% ('quite possible'), and consistent with the BSI estimate of 15 years that 'could shrink to 10 or even less'. Use it for data that must stay confidential for decades, where being wrong is expensive.
